title: The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts
content:
## 2.3 The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

FIELDWISE is a single-researcher European Fellowship hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) with a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, and the importance of its results rests not on the size of the action but on the generality of what a small, tightly-scoped action can demonstrate. Where sub-section 2.1 concerns the fellow's own development and 2.2 concerns the machinery that carries the results to their audiences, this sub-section states how those results make a difference beyond their immediate scope — beyond one crop, one host institution and one growing season — and sizes that difference against the call's expected impacts, with quantified indicators wherever a credible and honest number is available. The project addresses a problem of genuine European magnitude: approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, referenced to the European Environment Agency, and climate change is expected both to increase the agricultural area requiring irrigation and to raise irrigation demand where irrigation is already practised, so that the timing of irrigation decisions is a lever on a continent-scale resource problem. FIELDWISE does not claim to solve that problem; it changes the way one class of decision-support technology is built, evaluated and transferred, and the value of that change is what the paragraphs below quantify. Each contribution is anchored to the project's eleven KPIs (K1 to K11), each of which fixes a verifiable target on a named project output, so that magnitude is asserted against measurable commitments rather than rhetorically.

### Scientific impact and its reach beyond the project

The project's primary scientific contribution is a framework for agricultural AI evaluated according to temporal, geographic and operational transferability rather than only retrospective accuracy, and, additionally, a methodological bridge between high-information proximal hyperspectral observations and scalable Sentinel-based prediction. The importance of this is that it is not confined to processing tomato or to the two study regions: the failure mode it corrects — models that score well on retrospective metrics such as R², RMSE or classification accuracy yet transfer poorly to new seasons, new regions and real farms — is generic to accuracy-centred agricultural machine learning, so a demonstrated, reusable alternative evaluation discipline is of interest to the wider agricultural remote-sensing and agricultural-AI community well beyond FIELDWISE's own experiments. The magnitude of this contribution is made concrete and durable by three openly released assets rather than by publications alone: the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2), released with an explicit transferable or hyperspectral-only verdict recorded against every candidate feature (K2); the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2), released with a published model card (K4) and reporting calibration and prediction-interval coverage at forecast horizons t+1, t+3 and t+5 (K3); and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3), which states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to re-fit the model to a new agro-environment (K6). These map directly to the call's expected impacts of an enriched, more inter-connected European R&I culture and of increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations, and the last of them — a stated minimum calibration cost — is precisely what converts a locally trained model into an asset other European groups can re-use at a known, bounded cost, which is the mechanism by which the scientific contribution propagates beyond the immediate scope.

### Economic and technological impact

The economic and technological importance of FIELDWISE lies in its deliberate advancement of the work from a desktop research prototype to a scientifically validated web MVP, and in the fact that its readiness for real use is judged not by the project itself but by an external, non-academic evaluator. The DrR web MVP (D5.1) is a reachable tool serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution (K7); the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4) assesses it against real agricultural-software requirements across all nine assessment dimensions (K9); and the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5) names the required interfaces and the concrete post-fellowship steps for embedding the engine in farm-management information systems (K10). The importance of this chain is that it makes the route to economic uptake explicit and independently tested rather than asserted, which is the specific remedy to the previous submission's finding that the economic and technological route to users was insufficiently substantiated. The economic relevance of the target problem is itself substantial: water scarcity already produces agricultural yield losses and higher water costs in Europe, irrigation demand is expected to increase under climate change, and processing tomato is a high-value horticultural crop in which improved irrigation timing can therefore carry substantial agronomic and economic relevance. The magnitude of the available exploitation channel is unusually favourable for a single-fellow action because the non-academic partner is not a laboratory but a company whose farm-management information system is reported to be in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria — the two countries FIELDWISE works in — so the roadmap it writes from inside the implementing company points at an existing operational footprint rather than a hypothetical market. This substantiates the call's expected impact of strengthened R&I competitiveness and knowledge-transfer capacity of participating organisations; it is presented as the scale of the route to users, not as a promise of adoption within the fellowship, which the project explicitly does not make.

### Societal and environmental impact

The societal and environmental contribution follows from the same mechanism seen from the public side. By improving the timing and spatial prioritisation of irrigation decisions, FIELDWISE contributes to the EU-level opportunity for water savings in irrigated agriculture. Importantly, and as a matter of credibility rather than modesty, the project does not claim in advance that it will achieve a particular percentage reduction in water use; the environmental benefit will be quantified from project evidence rather than pre-declared. This discipline is deliberate: an MSCA-PF action with one fellow and a 30-month horizon cannot honestly commit to a headline water-saving number, and stating one would weaken rather than strengthen the impact case. What the project can commit to, and does, is the field-level measurement that makes any later saving assessable — the Field Decision Value report (D5.3) computes decision value for at least two competing models and reports lead time, false action rate and missed stress rate (K8), so that model choice is driven by operational usefulness rather than retrospective fit. Beyond the environmental route, the societal reach of the action is broadened by two public-facing measures the project commits to as activities: one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers and one public-facing article per year, which serve the call's expected impact of broadened public engagement with research and innovation and which, being operator-decided activities, carry no deliverable identifier of their own. The results are also carried into education through the co-design and delivery of a module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, serving the expected impact on the feedback of research results into teaching; and, at the level of the individual researcher, the fellowship's contribution to improved employability and career mobility within and beyond academia — carried by the Career Development Plan (D1.3) and the inter-sectoral placement, and argued in full in 2.1 — feeds the call's broader societal aim of a more dynamic and flexible European research talent base. Convergence of researcher working conditions with the European Charter for Researchers is evidenced at instrument level by the Career Development Plan (D1.3) and by ELTE's recruitment and researcher-development policies; no HR Excellence in Research accreditation is claimed.

### The European dimension and replicability

The distinctively European importance of FIELDWISE is that its architecture directly investigates whether agricultural AI developed in one European environment can be transferred to another. The MATE-to-MVCRI design tests this concretely — the Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report (D4.2) reports both zero-shot and locally calibrated performance (K5) — but the contribution reaches past these two sites, because the question it answers is the general one of how locally developed agricultural intelligence can become reliably transferable rather than remaining confined to the field in which it was trained. This is why the Adaptation protocol (D4.3), by stating the minimum local calibration required to move the model to a new agro-environment, is as much a European-impact instrument as a scientific one: it turns a Hungary-to-Bulgaria result into a re-usable recipe for adaptation to other European growing regions, so the magnitude of the contribution is bounded below by the two tested regions and, through the protocol, extensible to others at a stated cost. The cross-country, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary character of the action — international transfer with MVCRI, inter-sectoral evaluation and placement with AgroVIR, and the two-way transfer between plant physiology and geoinformatics between the fellow and ELTE — is exactly the profile the call associates with strengthened European research collaboration.

### Magnitude, importance and the discipline of the quantified claim

Taken together, the project's contribution is proportionate to a single-fellow action yet structured so that its importance is not: the transferability-first evaluation framework, the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel bridge, the reusable transfer library, model card and adaptation protocol, the externally evaluated MVP and the named FMIS integration route are each designed to outlive the fellowship and to be picked up by others. The magnitude of each claim is disciplined by an explicit KPI, so an evaluator can check the commitment rather than take the ambition on trust: five integrated seasons (K1), an explicit transferability verdict on every candidate feature (K2), three evaluated forecast horizons (K3), a published model card (K4), a reported zero-shot and calibrated cross-country gap (K5), a stated adaptation cost (K6), a reachable MVP (K7), decision value computed for at least two models (K8), a nine-dimension external evaluation (K9), a defined integration path (K10), and a career plan agreed and reviewed on a fixed cadence (K11). Where a number would be credible and meaningful — the extent of European water scarcity, the horizons at which forecasts are issued, the dimensions on which the tool is externally assessed, the operational footprint of the exploitation channel — the project states it; where a number could only be guessed — the eventual water saving — it refuses to pre-commit and instead builds the measurement that will supply the number honestly. That combination of demonstrable reach and refusal to over-claim is the substance of FIELDWISE's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts.

The project's magnitude is disciplined by eleven KPIs (K1 to K11), each fixing a verifiable target on a named output, including five integrated seasons, forecast horizons t+1/t+3/t+5, and a nine-dimension external evaluation.

The action's international (MVCRI), inter-sectoral (AgroVIR) and interdisciplinary (physiology-geoinformatics, fellow-ELTE) character matches the collaboration profile the call associates with strengthened European research collaboration.
